newsitem.title: USA: Ex-Fed officials doubt pre-Sept 24 Fed rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Fed officials doubt pre-Sept 24 Fed rate hike.

text.p: A Federal Reserve interest-rate hike ahead of its upcoming September 24 policy meeting is possible but highly unlikely, according to several former Fed officials interviewed on Thursday.
Fears of inter-meeting central bank action have been fanned in recent weeks by a spate of healthy data and evidence in the July policy meeting minutes that the committee adopted a tightening bias.

A September 3 Wall Street Journal article which suggested the possibility of a 50 basis point rate hike, and the prospect of sturdy gains in Friday's nervously-awaited August employment release, have only exacerbated these fears.
As the ex-Fed officials indicated however, the central bank has made pains to establish a pattern of regular post-meeting rate announcements in recent years.
In order to break this trend, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan would likely require overwhelming evidence of third quarter strength as well as concrete signs of an inflation danger, they said.
"I think an inter-meeting move is a very low probability," said Lyle Gramley, a former Fed governor and currently a consulting economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association.

"The committee's modus operandi since early 1994 has been to change policy only at the meetings rather than between meetings. If we were to get a payrolls increase of 300,000 or more when the numbers are reported (on Friday) I would increase the probability, but I still think it's probably less than 50-50." Gramley said the fact that the next rate hike would represent a shift in the direction of monetary policy made an inter-meeting move even less likely.

In minutes from the July 2-3 meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) adopted a so called "assymetric directive" for tightening, essentially allowing leeway for an inter-meeting hike. Economists are nearly unanimous in their belief that the bias was kept in place at the Fed's last policy meeting on August 20.

"I would think there is a lot of pressure (to tighten) based on the minutes of the last meeting available," said John LaWare, a former Fed governor who is now with the Boston firm Associated Industries. "If that has built up further, there could be some pressure to do something in the interim."

However, the last time the Fed moved between meetings was on April 18, 1994, when no tightening bias was in place. Since that date, several asymmetric directives have been set without prompting any inter-meeting move.
And LaWare stressed the Fed would be hesitant to move in the immediate aftermath of any single indicator -- such as payrolls -- as some market economists have suggested.

"They don't like to have the world think that they move on the basis of one statistic," he said. LaWare echoed other former Fed officials in stressing the committee's preference for waiting until after the presidential elections.
"It's a time of year when any central bank, not just the Fed, likes to keep its head down," said a former senior Fed official who declined to be named.
"And an inter-meeting move really is bells and whistles and bright lights and lightning bolts -- even more so than a move at a meeting. It's calling the whole world's attention."
